children: Regional attacks have disrupted shipping activity through the strategic waterway, pushing reported movements well below the recent 10-day average

Vessel traffic through the Strait of Hormuz fell to four on Tuesday, sharply below the waterway’s 10-day average of 18, as attacks in the region intensified. The figure was also down from seven vessels recorded a day earlier.

Two vessels exited the waterway while two entered, according to preliminary shipping data cited by Reuters on Wednesday. The decline comes as shipping activity through the strategic waterway remains subdued following the escalation of the Iran war.

The Strait of Hormuz handled around one-fifth of the world’s oil and liquefied natural gas supply before the war. The latest figures show significantly reduced reported vessel movements through the waterway, although some ships may not be captured in the data.

No very large crude carriers or liquefied natural gas tankers were among Tuesday’s recorded transits. Some vessels may be sailing through the waterway with their transponders switched off and would therefore not be counted in the reported figures.

One very large gas carrier, Salute, exited through the Iranian route carrying around 470,000 barrels of liquefied petroleum gas. Panamax-sized tanker Nautilus also exited, carrying around 510,000 barrels of naphtha through an unknown dark route.

The two vessels that entered the Strait of Hormuz on Tuesday were both laden, according to the preliminary shipping data. One was a short-range dirty products tanker, while the other was a dry bulk carrier, with both entering through the Iranian route.

The recorded movements included vessels carrying liquefied petroleum gas and naphtha, while no very large crude carriers or LNG tankers were reported among the four transits. The data therefore showed limited movement through the waterway on Tuesday.

Meanwhile, vessel traffic through the Bab el-Mandeb Strait remained relatively stable on Tuesday, with 22 ships recorded sailing through the waterway. The figure was only slightly lower than the 24 vessels recorded a day earlier.

The latest figures show a sharp decline in reported traffic through the Strait of Hormuz compared with its recent 10-day average. However, the presence of vessels travelling with transponders switched off means actual traffic through the waterway may be higher than reported.
